title: Egypt's Power Will Be Broken
overview: Ezekiel announces that Babylon will crush Egypt and its allies, ending the power that the people of Judah had hoped would rescue them.

parts.label: Egypt's dark day (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: The "day of the LORD" here means the moment God acts in judgment, and this time it is aimed at Egypt and the nations fighting alongside it. The list names Egypt's neighbors and hired soldiers, and the last group is most likely people of Judah who had fled to Egypt, though scholars are not certain.

parts.label: Allies fall, Cush panics (vv. 6-9)
parts.note: The places named in verse 6 mark Egypt's far borders, so the sword will reach the whole country. Messengers rushing up the Nile by boat picture the news of Egypt's fall shocking Cush (roughly modern Sudan), which felt safe far to the south.

parts.label: Babylon as the tool (vv. 10-12)
parts.note: God names Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and his ruthless army as the means of this judgment, while still calling them wicked. Egypt lived on the Nile and its canals, so drying up its waters pictures the collapse of everything the land depended on.

parts.label: City by city (vv. 13-19)
parts.note: Naming cities from Thebes in the far south to Pelusium on the northeast border says no part of Egypt will escape, and neither its gods nor its rulers will save it. Babylon did later attack Egypt, but surviving records do not describe ruin on this scale, so many read these lines as the heightened language of war poetry.

parts.label: Pharaoh's broken arms (vv. 20-26)
parts.note: This message is dated to early 587 BC by most counts, while Babylon was besieging Jerusalem and after Pharaoh's army had failed to drive it off. An arm stood for military strength, so breaking both arms means Egypt will lose all power to fight while Babylon grows stronger.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether this was fulfilled in Babylon's actual campaigns against Egypt or is poetic war language, and some also read the "day of the LORD" here as a preview of a final judgment on all nations.
think: How can anyone tell the difference between strength that is real and strength that only looks impressive?
